faqs.a: eMAG trained a generation of Romanian shoppers to compare before they buy, and that behavior spills into every sector. Your pages should answer the comparison questions upfront: what is included, what it costs, how you differ from the cheaper option. faqs.q: How does eMAG change the way I should do SEO in Romania?

I usually recommend winning your home city first, then expanding into Bucharest once the revenue from local wins funds the bigger fight.
faqs.q: Should I target Bucharest first or focus on my own city?

I build a review routine into your operation so fresh proof keeps arriving without you having to chase it.
faqs.q: How do Romanian customers check a business before buying?

faqs.a: The most common ones: publishing English content and machine-translating it into Romanian, ignoring diacritics in URLs and headings, stuffing Bucharest keywords onto pages that serve other cities, and running a Google Business Profile with the wrong category. h1: SEO Expert in Romania: Win the Romanian Searches Your Competitors Ignore
intro:
If you run a business in Romania, your customers are searching for what you sell right now, in Romanian, on Google. That sentence sounds obvious, but most Romanian businesses still act like it is not true. They have a website that was translated from English, or built five years ago and never touched, while a competitor down the street collects the calls. Romania is the largest EU country in Southeastern Europe by population, with around 19 million people, and its internet economy has been accelerating for a decade. Bucharest concentrates the money, the multinationals and the agencies. Cluj-Napoca has grown into the country's second tech capital, full of software companies and startups. Timisoara anchors the west with automotive software and engineering, and Iasi does the same in the northeast with IT and outsourcing. Together these four cities hold most of the country's commercial search demand, and in three of them, proper SEO is still rare enough that a well-run campaign can win fast.

The Romanian buyer is a specific animal and you have to respect how they shop. eMAG, the dominant ecommerce platform, trained millions of Romanians to compare prices, read reviews and check ratings before spending a single leu. That comparison habit does not stop at products. When someone in Bucharest needs a lawyer, a dentist or a renovation crew, they open Google, compare the top results, read the reviews, and only then call. They are price-aware but not cheap: they will pay for quality once they understand what they are paying for. Vague pages that hide pricing lose to clear pages that explain value. This is why generic SEO advice imported from the US or UK underperforms here. It was written for buyers who behave differently.

Language is the other half of the story. Romanian dominates local search, and Romanian has diacritics that change meaning: s and t with a comma below appear in everyday words. Search engines handle them, but most business websites do not. They publish in English, or they machine-translate, and they wonder why they never rank for the queries real customers type. I plan every campaign around genuine Romanian keyword research, and the pages read naturally to native speakers because they are written for them from the start, not converted afterward.

The competitive picture is the good news. Google handles the overwhelming majority of Romanian searches, so there is one battlefield, not five. Outside Bucharest, most local competitors have thin websites, incomplete Google Business Profiles and almost no reviews. That is a gap you can drive through. I work as a one-person studio, which means you get the person doing the work, not an account manager relaying messages. The audit is free, the plan is written in plain language, and the first wins usually show up where the competition is thinnest: your own city, in your own language.

section1.body:
Citations are the boring foundation that rankings are built on, and in Romania most businesses have a cracked one. Your business is listed in dozens of places across the web: Google Business Profile, Pagini Aurii (the Romanian Yellow Pages), Yelp, Facebook, sector-specific directories, old portals nobody remembers signing up for. Over the years those listings drift. An old address here, a tracking phone number there, a duplicate profile from when the business changed names. Google cross-checks your name, address and phone number everywhere it can find them, and when the listings disagree, Google trusts you less. In a market where few competitors have clean citations, cleaning yours is a genuine competitive advantage.

My citation work for Romanian businesses follows a fixed order. First, the Google Business Profile gets claimed, verified and fully completed: correct primary category in Romanian search terms, every relevant secondary category, services listed, real photos, accurate hours including holiday schedules. Second, I audit the full citation footprint and fix inconsistencies, starting with the directories that actually matter in Romania: Pagini Aurii, Yelp Romania, Facebook, and the sector directories for your trade. I skip the junk directories that exist only to sell links, because they do nothing for rankings and can create more mess than they solve. Every listing ends up with the same +40 phone number, the same address format, and the same business name spelling, diacritics included.

Then there is the review layer, which in Romania sits on top of citations like a multiplier. Pagini Aurii and Google both show ratings, and Romanian buyers are trained by ecommerce to filter by them. I set up a simple review routine for your business: the right ask at the right moment after a job is done, a direct link that makes leaving a review take thirty seconds, and genuine replies to every review that arrives. Over months this compounds into the kind of public proof that makes choosing you feel obvious. Citations get you into the consideration set; reviews win the comparison. I build both, because in Romania you need both.

section2.body:
For most local searches in Romania, the buying decision happens before anyone reaches a website. The map pack shows three businesses, and the customer picks from those three. That is the whole game for local SEO here, and it is why I treat your Google Business Profile as your most important web property, not an afterthought. Romanian searchers use queries like 'instalator Bucuresti', 'stomatolog Cluj preturi' and 'restaurant langa mine', and the businesses that win those queries share the same traits: complete profiles, correct categories, recent reviews, real photos, and posts that show the business is alive.

Optimizing a profile for the Romanian market has specific details that generic guides miss. Categories need to match how Romanians search, not how Google translates your trade into English. Service areas need to reflect real travel patterns: someone in Cluj-Napoca will drive to Floresti but not to Turda for most services, and your profile should say so. Opening hours need to be accurate down to the Saturday schedule, because 'deschis acum' (open now) filtering is heavily used and wrong hours lose you the click at the exact moment of intent. Photos need to show the real business, the real team, the real work, because Romanian buyers have learned to distrust stock photography the same way they distrust vague pricing.

Reviews are the tiebreaker in the Romanian map pack, and the dynamics are specific. A profile with 4.5 stars and fifty genuine reviews will outrank an older competitor with twelve reviews, even if that competitor has been around longer. Recency matters: a review from last month counts more than one from two years ago. I build the review engine into your daily operation so it runs without willpower: QR codes on invoices, a direct link sent by SMS after the job, replies to everything within a day. And because Romania is a market where word travels fast in professional circles, I make sure your responses to negative reviews are calm, specific and solution-oriented. Handled well, a critical review answered properly converts better than a page of five-star praise.

why.body:
Romania looks like a standard European market from a distance, and that is exactly why most SEO campaigns fail here. They are built on assumptions that do not hold. The first wrong assumption is language. Around 19 million people live in Romania, and the commercial searches that matter are typed in Romanian, with Romanian diacritics, using Romanian phrasing. 'Cel mai bun' beats 'best', 'preturi' beats 'pricing', and a page written in English and run through a translator will never feel native to the buyer or rank like a native page. I have seen businesses spend thousands on English content aimed at Romanian customers and get nothing, because the customers were never searching in English in the first place.

The second wrong assumption is buyer behavior. The Romanian buyer compares. Years of shopping on eMAG trained the whole market to check prices, read reviews and look for the catch before committing. This makes Romanian buyers slower to convert but more loyal once they choose you, and it changes what your pages must do. Your service pages need to answer the comparison questions: what is included, what does it cost, why are you not the cheapest option. Pages that hide behind 'contact us for a quote' lose to pages that explain value openly. I write for this buyer deliberately, because content that respects how Romanians decide converts at a multiple of content that does not.

The third wrong assumption is competition. Bucharest is competitive, genuinely so, with agencies fighting over the big accounts. But Romania is not Bucharest. Cluj-Napoca, Timisoara, Iasi, Brasov, Constanta and Oradea all have growing commercial demand and a fraction of the SEO competition. In these cities, the typical competitor has a dated website, an unclaimed or half-finished Google Business Profile, and a handful of reviews. A focused campaign with proper Romanian keyword research, clean citations and a working review system can take meaningful positions in months, not years. That is the playbook I run: win the city you can win fastest, convert that into revenue and proof, then expand. It is slower than promising the moon on day one, and it is the approach that actually works in this market.
